nameStory: This tiny mushroom gets its name from its incredibly thin, hair-like stem that looks almost like a delicate thread or capillary. The word 'capillaris' comes from the Latin for 'hair-like,' perfectly describing these mushrooms that seem to sprout from fallen leaves on the finest possible stalks.
description: The Hair-stemmed Pinwheel is one of New England's tiniest mushrooms, with caps barely the size of a pencil eraser or smaller. These delicate fungi pop up in groups on decaying oak leaves, looking like miniature umbrellas on impossibly thin, wiry stems. The small caps start rounded but develop a shallow depression in the center with radiating lines, giving them their pinwheel appearance. They're so small you might walk right past them, but once you spot one, you'll often find many more nearby.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Extremely thin and wiry, less than 1mm thick but up to 2.4 inches long, with a distinctive shiny, almost polished appearance that catches the light

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Tiny convex caps only 2-15mm across that develop a central depression with radiating furrows, creating a pinwheel or parachute-like pattern

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows directly on decaying oak leaves, often in small groups scattered across the leaf litter

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White spore print, though getting enough spores from these tiny mushrooms requires patience and several specimens

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Remarkably small overall - you could fit several caps on your thumbnail with room to spare

habitat: Look for these tiny mushrooms in oak forests and mixed woodlands throughout New England, always on decaying oak leaves. They prefer shaded areas with consistent moisture where oak leaf litter accumulates, from lowland forests to mid-elevation slopes. You'll find them scattered across the forest floor wherever oak trees drop their leaves.

seasonality.spring: Not typically fruiting yet, though mycelium may be active in the warming leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season, especially after warm summer rains when humidity is high and oak leaves are decomposing actively.
seasonality.fall: Continue fruiting into early fall, particularly abundant after autumn rains on freshly fallen oak leaves.
seasonality.winter: Dormant period with no visible mushrooms, though the mycelium persists in the leaf litter.

funFact: These mushrooms are so incredibly resilient that their wiry stems can be bent almost into a complete circle without breaking - a superpower that helps them bounce back from being stepped on or blown around by wind!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Collared Parachute (Marasmius rotula), but Hair-stemmed Pinwheels are noticeably smaller, darker, and lack the distinctive white collar around the stem base that gives the Collared Parachute its name. Memory trick: 'Capillaris is smaller and collar-less.'
contextualKnowledge: This species belongs to a group of mushrooms called 'pinwheels and parachutes' because of their distinctive radial cap patterns. Don't let the delicate appearance fool you - these tiny decomposers play a crucial role in breaking down tough oak leaves and recycling nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.
compareHints: Among its Marasmius relatives, Hair-stemmed Pinwheel is distinguished by being both the smallest and having the thinnest stems. While Collared Parachute has similar radial furrows, it's larger and lighter colored with a distinctive collar. Fairy Ring Marasmius grows in grass rather than on leaves and is much larger with a completely different habitat preference.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Marasmius relatives in New England, the collared parachute is distinguished by its unique gill-to-collar attachment and preference for small woody debris.
Fairy ring marasmius stands out from other Marasmius species by its robust size and grassland habitat - most of its relatives are tiny and grow on dead wood or leaves.
